newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: French kill rebel in fresh Central Africa clash.
newsitem.headline: French kill rebel in fresh Central Africa clash.

text.p: French troops fought a gunbattle with mutinous Central African Republic soldiers in the capital Bangui on Thursday, killing one rebel and capturing another, the French army said.
A military statement said there were no French casualties.

The gunbattle broke out as mediators tackling the two-month army rebellion in Bangui recommended the use of African troops to separate rebel soldiers and loyalist troops and disarm civilians, a negotiator said on Thursday.

It was the most serious clash in the troubled capital since French troops, based in the former colony under defence accords, killed 10 rebels on January 5 in reprisal for the shooting death of two French officers.

The French military spokesman in Bangui, Colonel Henry Pelissier, told Reuters the armed group that ambushed the French patrol were believed to be elements of the mutineers out of control of their own leaders.

"This afternoon there ware road blocks set up on the road leading to the French ambassador's residence," he said. But he added he did not think the incident marked a new flareup in the two-month-old mutiny.

The military statement said: "At 1545, just after the Ndri cemetery, two km (1.2 mile) north of the Kassai Barracks, a French army patrol came under attack by a group of 12 mutineers, including a lieutenant and a sergeant."
It said the rebels were armed with AK-47 rifles, rocket-propelled grenades and hand grenades.
The French patrol returned fire, killed one rebel and captured another and seized firearms and ammunition.

Earlier the Defence Ministry in Paris said France would back the proposed African force of about 300 men, which could be deployed in Bangui within weeks subject to approval by leaders of mediators Burkina Faso, Chad, Gabon and Mali.
"The final decision will be made by the four heads of state," said Colonel Alioune Ibaba, a member of the Malian-led mediation team.
He told Reuters the force would be a buffer between rebels and loyalists who have clashed repeatedly since the country's third mutiny in less than a year erupted on November 15.
They would also monitor peace accords and, with the help of the United Nations, disarm civilian militias loyal to President Ange-Felix Patasse, Ibaba said.

"This phase (disarmament) is not limited to members of the mediation committee," Ibaba added. "After the approval of the four heads of state, interested countries, depending on their financial, material and human resources, can participate."
Scores of people have been killed in clashes between rebels and presidential guard troops, who are backed by French forces.
French troops fought bloody battles with rebels when they quelled a more violent mutiny in May last year, which followed one in April. Two French officers were killed in the latest uprising.

Grievances over pay and conditions turned into a campaign by predominantly southern mutineers to oust Patasse, a northerner who won elections in 1993. The mutiny has since degenerated into generalised ethnic feuding.
